scenes.text: [A] The next afternoon, Mom’s at another interview, and Halmoni naps through lunch—which is unusual, because even though Halmoni loves to sleep, she loves eating even more. [B] Sam’s upstairs on her computer, and I have nothing to do but snack on peanut butter cups, pace, and think about the tiger. [C] Here’s what I know: [D] 1.
The tiger found Halmoni. Or at least, the tiger found me, which means it will find Halmoni soon enough. [E] 2. Tigers are determined.

It wants the stories, and it will do whatever it takes to get them back. The kosa should have kept the tiger away, but I saw it in the library, so that obviously didn’t work. [F] 3. We need more protection, and even though talking about the tiger upsets Halmoni, I need to tell her.

[G] When I can’t pace any longer, I slip into Halmoni’s bedroom. The dust dances in the air, catching in the windowlight, and the misty light from outside makes the room hazy. It feels like I’ve stepped into a separate world, like a little mini universe, trapped in time. [H] I pull back the covers and gently shake my grandmother awake.
“Halmoni,” I whisper. “Halmoni, wake up.” [I] She mumbles and turns over in bed, so I shake her again. A little harder.
Maybe a little too hard. [J] She cracks her eyes open. “Lily Bean?” she murmurs. “You hungry?”

[K] “Not really,” I say. Honestly, I’m pretty full on peanut butter cups. [L] She climbs out of bed—slowly and intently, like she’s climbing out of quicksand. Sitting on the edge of the mattress, she stretches, and I can almost see the sleep sliding off her.
[A] She looks weak. [B] “Halmoni,” I blurt, my tiger questions temporarily on hold, “is the bug gone? Are you sure you’re okay?” [C] “I am better than okay.
My family is here. That is all I ever want.” She smiles, but her words wobble. “You stop worry.” [D] “Speaking of worrying .
. .” I tug at one of my braids. “I think we need more protection than just kosa. I saw the tiger again.”

[E] For a second, fear ignites in Halmoni’s eyes. But then she closes them and shakes her head. When her eyes open again, she is soft and smiling. [F] She opens her nightstand drawer and pulls out a sheaf of dried herbs.
Then she breaks off a piece and places it in my palm. “This for you. This make you safe, okay? So you don’t worry anymore.”
[G] I stare at the shriveled plant and look up at her. “What is it?” [H] “This mugwort,” she explains. “This my medicine to eat, but you don’t eat.
You keep in you pockets, and it give you protection.” [I] I thank her and slip the dried herb into my pocket. [J] “And this . .

.” She hesitates before reaching behind her neck and unlatching the necklace. The silver chain with the pearl pendant—her special necklace, the one she wears every day, the one she rubs between her fingers when she’s trying to find the right English words. “This help, too. You wear for protection, and it keep you safe.”
[K] My pulse beats in every limb as she fastens it around my neck. It’s heavier than it looks. “But this is yours,” I say. [A] “Yes, and now it is yours.”
[B] I press my palm against the pendant. It’s warmer than I expected. It warms my chest, and I like the way it feels, heavy above my heart. “Did this really keep you safe?”
[C] “I am here, yes?” [D] I pinch the pearl between my fingers, and it seems to buzz with energy. “But what about you? Don’t you still need protection?
The tigers are hunting.” [E] She smiles, but it’s not a regular Halmoni smile. It doesn’t match her eyes. “I be safe, Lily.

I am not worrying.” [F] I’m not so sure, and when she sees that in my eyes, she says, “Okay, we go grocery now. We get even more protection, extra help against bad spirits. We buy pine nuts to burn and rice to scatter under full moon.
Also, I need fresh ingredient for rice cake.” [G] I smile, feeling better. [H] She leans closer. “And I buy you favorite treats, because I am best.” She pauses.
“Well, you mother is best. But . . .
I am best best.” [I] I laugh. “You are.” [J] She raises an eyebrow.

“Now go tell Sam.” [K] After I call Sam downstairs and tell her where we’re going, she leans on the dining table, crossing her arms. “That’s not a good idea. Didn’t Mom say you’re not supposed to drive?”
[L] Halmoni’s eyes dart away, and I get the urge to pinch my sister. Sam is a black hole for happiness. [M] “You can drive if you want,” I tell Sam. [N] She recoils.
“I don’t know. . . .” She could drive.

She has her permit, and Halmoni’s a licensed driver. Mom keeps bugging Sam to practice. [A] But, of course, she won’t. Sam tried two lessons with her driving instructor and refused to get behind the wheel after that.
Nothing bad happened, but she won’t do it because of Dad’s car accident. [B] Halmoni presses her palm against Sam’s cheek. “Life is not for waiting. We go now.
We be okay.” [C] Sam tugs at her white streak. “But Mom said—” [D] Halmoni tsks.
“You mother don’t know what she says. I be fine.” [E] Sam looks unsure, which is ridiculous, because Sam never cares what Mom says. [F] “You can stay here,” I tell her.
[G] There’s a flash of hurt in her eyes, and then annoyance. “No. I’ll come,” she says. [H] Halmoni claps.
“Good girls! I go change into fancy clothes.” [I] Sam frowns. “Why?”
[J] “Grocery,” Halmoni answers before disappearing into her room. [K] Sam shakes her head, but a tiny smiles tugs at her lips. And I feel happy, too. Halmoni is Halmoni.
Weird is her normal. And I don’t have to worry. With one hand, I pat the mugwort in my pocket. With the other, I grasp my pendant.

Everything will be okay. I just know it. [L] We arrive at the grocery store with a short list: [M] For eating: • mochi flour, for rice cakes • wasabi peas, for Mom • Happy Nut crackers, for Sam • peanut butter cups, for Lily

[N] For extra protection: • five-grain rice, to scatter in the woods • pine nuts, to burn under a full moon [O] For misc.: • laundry detergent [P] Sam raises an eyebrow when she sees the protection category, but she doesn’t say anything. [A] “We have to leave here in half hour, because rain coming soon,” Halmoni says.
[B] Sam frowns. “It’s not gonna rain today. The weather app says there’s a zero percent chance.” [C] Halmoni just pats Sam’s head.
“Half hour.” [D] “That’s fine,” I say. “We won’t take that long.” [E] I’m about to head off to check the grains aisle, when a woman with bright red curly hair runs right up to us.
[F] “You must be the granddaughters!” she squeals. I’m a little worried she’s about to pinch our cheeks, but she refrains. [G] Halmoni beams. “These my little ones.”
[H] “Your grandmother is the greatest,” the woman gushes to Sam and me. “She cured my asthma with her plants.” [I] Sam takes a very small step back. “That’s cool.”

[J] The woman stays to chat with Halmoni for a while, and when she finally flits away, a bald man tells us that Halmoni made him laugh, even after his divorce. And then an older woman tells us that she plays cards with Halmoni. [K] It’s a lot to take in, especially when I’m on a protection-finding mission. [L] Halmoni introduces Sam and me to everybody she sees, and they all tell us how pretty we are, how sweet.
I try to keep track of everyone, but their names slip through my mind, their faces blur together. [M] Halmoni is so popular here. Everybody knows her. Everybody loves her.
And I have no idea who these people are. [N] After about twenty minutes, Sam pulls me into the cereal aisle to hide. [O] “Halmoni tricked us,” she says. “This isn’t a quick grocery run.
This is a whole event.” [A] “She knows everyone,” I say. [B] “Yeah, which explains the nice clothes, I guess.” Sam grins. [C] “Halmoni has a lot of friends,” I say, checking our list.
I guess there’s no harm in waiting for Halmoni. [D] Sam plops down on the floor. “There are so many people we don’t know. And they all have a story about her.

It’s like she has a secret life.” [E] I join her, sitting on the tiles and leaning against the store-brand frosted flakes. I don’t say anything, but she knows I agree. Our sister telepathy hasn’t disappeared completely.
[F] I pick at the stitching of my jeans. “Speaking of stories . . .” I wait for Sam to roll her eyes, but she doesn’t, so I continue.
“Halmoni told me this weird one I’d never heard. About tigers.” [G] Sam raises an eyebrow, a silent Go on. [H] I take a deep breath.

“You know how Halmoni always said that the stars were made of stories? Well, apparently that’s true. And the tigers used to guard them. But Halmoni stole some of the stars and hid them in jars or something.
And now the tigers are mad.” [I] Sam frowns. “That’s a weird story, Lily. Halmoni’s crazy.”
[J] “She’s not crazy. Don’t say that. But anyway, she said—” [K] “When did she tell you all this?”

[L] “The first night we were here, but—” [M] Her eyes fall to the pendant around my neck. “And when did she give you that?” [N] Automatically, my hand flies to my chest, covering it—as if it’s something to hide.

“Just now, before we left. She was talking about different kinds of protection.” [A] Sam unties and then reties her shoelaces for no apparent reason. “I don’t know why she never talks to me about this stuff.”

[B] I didn’t realize that Sam wanted Halmoni to tell her stuff. [C] For a second, I consider telling Sam everything—about how I saw a tiger that should be impossible. And about how I chased that tiger, even though I knew it was dangerous—and I still can’t really explain why. [D] But then I hear a familiar voice in the next aisle.
“Maybe we could make muffins or cupcakes or something? Like we could use Mom’s recipe. Or the sticky buns she used to make?” [E] It’s Ricky.

[F] When I rise to my feet and press my ear against the cereal boxes, Sam gives me a look that says, What is wrong with you? [G] I don’t have any answer to that. I know it’s wrong to eavesdrop, but for some reason, I don’t stop myself. [H] Maybe it’s because Ricky is sticky.
Or maybe it’s just because I’m nosy. Or maybe it’s because Ricky was there when I saw the tiger. [I] I tiptoe down the aisle until I reach the end. There’s a big BUY TWO, GET ONE FREE!

display of Lucky Charms—about a hundred stacked cereal boxes—and I use it as a spy shield. I peek out around the side. [J] Invisible, I tell myself, calling on my superpower with all my might. [K] Ricky walks down the aisle with a man who I’m guessing is his dad, because he looks like a grown-up version of Ricky—same messy brown hair, same big blue eyes.

I wonder if Ricky’s great-grandfather looked like that, too. The tiger hunter. [A] Sam frowns in confusion and follows me to the end of the aisle. “Lily?” she asks, but I shush her, and she joins me in spying.
[B] “Who’s that?” she whispers. [C] I shake my head so she’ll be quiet, but she nudges me in the ribs. Sam is incapable of being invisible. [D] “I met him at the library,” I say, as quietly as I can.

[E] Sam makes a hmm noise, a noise that says she knows something I don’t know, which is annoying, but I ignore her. I’m busy eavesdropping. [F] “Connor loves that recipe,” Ricky’s saying. He’s looking up at his dad with a kind of desperation, but his dad’s not paying attention.
“Did I tell you about that one time when I made it, he ate like four whole servings? No, not like four. Like six, actually. Then he got really sick and he threw up everywhere and—”
[G] “Ricky, quiet.” Ricky’s dad massages his temples. [H] I get this sinking, glued-to-the-ground feeling. This is an awkward family moment. I should mind my own business.
[I] “We probably shouldn’t . . . ,” Sam murmurs, but I keep watching.

[J] Ricky’s dad pushes a cart, scanning the canned goods, and Ricky jogs along after him. “But, Dad, I’m pretty sure I told you this story. Do you remember? It was when we were at the laser tag place, and—”

[K] “Ricky,” his dad snaps, so loudly that Sam and I both step back from the cereal. [L] Ricky looks up at him, face open and hopeful, like he can’t tell his dad is upset with him. “And I shot him right in the chest. With the laser only, so it’s not like he could actually feel it, and then—”
[A] “Will you just shut up?” [B] The words echo through me. I feel the horribleness of them in my chest, squeezing hard. [C] Sam tugs at my shirtsleeve.

“Come on,” she whispers. [D] I look over her shoulder to see Halmoni standing at the end of the aisle, basket full, waving us over. She points to her watch and mimes marching and then rain. The grocery store has mostly cleared out by now, and she’s worried about the weather.
[E] Gaja, Halmoni mouths. Let’s go. [F] But I can’t leave now. Staying feels wrong, but leaving feels even worse.

I inch closer, pressing myself against the Lucky Charms. [G] I watch Ricky stop walking, lips frozen midsmile but eyes wide with hurt. Slowly, his smile fades, and he stares down at his shoes. [H] I lean forward.
I don’t know this kid, but I know that feeling. I want to reach out and say, I see you. [I] I want to— [J] Only there’s no more time for wanting, because suddenly I’m falling forward.

[K] The cardboard display falls over, and then I’m on top of it, sprawled out on the floor in front of Ricky and his dad and the rest of the grocery store—surrounded by cereal boxes. [L] “Oh, man,” Sam says, backing away from me, as if embarrassment is contagious. [M] Down the aisle, Halmoni hurries toward me, but her hurrying isn’t very fast, and I’m just lying here on the floor. [N] I look up at Ricky and his dad, who look down at me, staring in surprise.
[O] Ricky blinks. “I know you.” [A] “Um,” I say. I try to manage a shrug that says something like Oh, hi, what a coincidence running into you here!

but is probably more like I was spying and heard your dad say shut up and now I’m lying on a mountain of cereal. [B] “Are you okay?” Ricky’s dad asks, looking both startled and concerned. [C] I nod. “Yeah, totally fine.
I was just . . . trying to decide if I wanted cereal.
But . . . I don’t think .
. . I’m going to . .
. get it?” [D] Ricky’s smile comes back, spreading slowly across his face. And it’s just a What is she even doing?
smile, but still. [E] Sam snorts. Which is rude. [F] I stand up and clear my throat.

“Bye!” [G] I’m very much ready to run away now, but Halmoni’s finally made it here, and she stops me. [H] Halmoni runs a hand over my hair—which is probably a mess—and beams at Ricky and his dad. “Hello, boys!”
[I] Ricky’s dad clears his throat. “Hello, Ae-Cha.” [J] Halmoni smiles at Ricky’s dad and points at the cereal. “You help me fix that, please?”
[K] He lurches forward and props the cardboard shelf up. It falls right back over. I guess completely crushing it ruined its ability to . .
. be a shelf. [L] “Sorry,” I mumble. [M] “All okay,” Halmoni says.

“We stack.” [N] So Halmoni, Sam, Ricky, his dad, and I work together, stacking the boxes. It’s incredibly uncomfortable. I want to disappear, because they don’t know that I was eavesdropping—but it’s obvious, right?
[A] When we’re done, Halmoni puts her hand on the dad’s shoulder. “Thank you,” she says. “It is always good to help each other when we need it.” [B] She turns to Ricky.
“See, I have struggle here, and you dad help me. Sometimes parents and grandparents need help, too.” [C] Sam and I exchange a glance. Now is not the time for one of Halmoni’s life lessons.
[D] Turning back to his dad, Halmoni says, “And when Ricky have struggle, you help him. We always remember to help each other. You both good boys, and you have hard times. I know that.
But when you have hard times, you come together, not apart. Okay?” [E] Halmoni glows with both fierceness and kindness. It’s like she’s lit up from the inside, like she has stars burning inside her.
[F] And I realize: she knows. She must. I’m not sure how she managed to overhear their conversation, but somehow she did. [G] Ricky and his dad both nod, and the dad looks a little embarrassed.

I think he knows he was wrong. Ricky looks over at me, and I shrug, as if I have no idea what Halmoni’s doing. [H] But really, I get it. I wanted to tell Ricky, I see you, but Halmoni’s talking to Ricky’s dad.

She’s telling him, I see you, and I see the way you could be. [I] Even though Halmoni’s fierceness had nothing to do with our tiger-protection plan, I can’t help thinking I was supposed to see this. This is part of her story.
